subject: Biotechnology
title: Polygenic Risk Scores
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Polygenic Risk Scores.

hook.text: Heart disease is not caused by one gene — it is the sum of thousands of small genetic effects. PRS adds them up.

buildup.text: GWAS identifies millions of variants each with tiny effects — polygenic risk scores combine them into one number.

discovery.text: Top 5% PRS for coronary artery disease face triple the average risk — comparable to single-gene disorders.

twist.text: PRS trained on European data perform poorly in African populations — diversity in training data is critical for equity.

climax.text: Combining PRS with clinical risk factors improves prediction — genetics plus lifestyle plus biomarkers together.

punchline.text: Thousands of genes, one score — polygenic risk quantifies inherited susceptibility.

quiz.question: Why do polygenic risk scores perform poorly across diverse populations?
options: Genetic variants linked to disease are identical in all populations
Scores trained on one population may not capture variants and effect sizes relevant in other ancestries
Diverse populations have fewer genetic variants overall

details.summary: Polygenic risk scores combine the effects of thousands of genetic variants to estimate an individual's risk for common diseases like heart disease, diabetes, and certain cancers. Each variant has a tiny effect, but together they create a meaningful risk prediction for complex diseases.
details.whyItMatters: Most common diseases are not caused by single genes but by many variants each contributing small effects. Polygenic risk scores capture this complexity, enabling risk stratification that could guide earlier screening and preventive interventions for
takeaways: PRS aggregate thousands of small-effect variants into a single risk score
They identify people at 3 to 5 times average risk for common diseases
Clinical implementation is growing for coronary artery disease and breast cancer

faq.question: How accurate are polygenic risk scores for predicting disease?
faq.answer: PRS typically explain 5 to 15 percent of disease risk variance, which is meaningful for population stratification but limited for individual prediction. People in the top 5 percent of PRS distribution have 3 to 5 times higher risk than average. They work best combined with clinical risk factors.

faq.question: Do polygenic risk scores work equally well across ancestries?
faq.answer: No. Most PRS were developed from European-ancestry populations and perform poorly in other groups. This creates health equity concerns as clinical implementation advances. Developing ancestry-appropriate scores using diverse populations is a major research priority to avoid exacerbating disparities.
